segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My name is Guy Soldier. My full name is Richard, Richard Soldier. They call me Guy. They gave me questions written down here for me to ask you. If you want to talk about something different, go ahead and talk about it. It’s going to be open for you to talk. You might know something interesting. You can talk about it – that's the kind of thing they're looking for. Growing up with our language, things that we heard about, and the names of things, is what they're looking for. So, you might know something we don't, so be ready to talk about it. The first is, what is your English name?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Ruby May Jackson.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Jackson, Ruby May. What about your Cherokee name?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I-tsi-wi U-ya-s-ga-wo-di.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I-tsi-wi, where does that come from?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Wa le li U-ya-s-ga-wo-di.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wa-le-li U-ya-s-ga-wo-di.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Charlie Shell.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Charlie Shell, U-ya-s-ga-wo-di, yeah U-ya-s-ga-wo-di.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: U-ya-s-ga-wo-di.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it u-tla-s-gu?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: U-ya-s-ga-wo-di.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Uh-huh, Shell.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh yeah, U-ya-s-ga-wo-di.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: U-ya-s-ga-wo-di.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I understand now. U-ya-s-ga-wo-di.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh OK, kind of like eggshell. Where were you born and what year?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: At Hastings?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: At the old building is where I was born.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There were a lot of them born there, ain't it?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I also had my child there, where I was born.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK. Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Chuculate.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, Chuculate.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Chuculate.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just around there.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I was born there right above Chuculate Church.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, the church.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: We would walk to church.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Walk down.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: When church was over, we would walk back up all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So that's where you all went?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: All the time on Sunday we would walk down.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Are you still going to church there?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Uh-huh, still.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It's really changed, hasn't it?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: It has changed a lot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I went there one time. A guy named Johnson Vann was the pastor.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: My sister was supposed to join me, that's her husband. Mary Johnson, that was her husband. Johnson.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Johnson, yeah. He was nice. Is that where you mostly grew up?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I grew up there. In ‘62 I graduated at Sequoyah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sequoyah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I graduated, and I lived there for years. If it wasn't for that Sequoyah, I would not have graduated. I’m happy for that. There was a school called Cave Springs. I started in ninth grade. I didn't like it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Eighth.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: When I was going to start 10th grade, I didn't want to go back to Cave Springs. My parents, both of them, I don't know, but I think my mother just went to the third grade, and my dad I'm not sure. They really wanted...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ...you to finish.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: For us to finish school. They did everything they could for us to go to school. When I didn't want to go to Cave Springs school, I told them, “If you don't send me to Sequoyah, I will not go to school.” I told them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you really learned over here.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I graduated. Also, I went to school at Northeastern.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I went to school there, too. They were really proud for us to be in school, there were a lot of us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Cherokees?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: There were 10 of us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I'll be.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Mom had one and Dad had two girls. There were 13 of us. They were half-siblings. They would tell us, “I don't want to hear you saying that, ‘my half-siblings.’ Just my siblings, that’s it.” They raised three of them. There's 10 of us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There was 10. What places did you work?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: There was a factory a long time ago, it was called Stilwell Foods, Stilwell canning.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, it used to be a canning factory.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I started working there. I continued school, then Cherokee Nation hired me. It was in ‘72, I think. It was in ‘72 when I started, I think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What did you do at Cherokee Nation? What part did you work at?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: A lot of places. Youth Service is where I was working and started. They have them in there. I think it's still running, they still put them in there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, what is that? Where they put the kids?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Where?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Cherokee Nation. Ah, what was it called?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I don't know. Indian Child Services, or what?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I forgot.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Child services or what?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The building that was by the Cherokee Nation complex. For instance, the Donated Foods, the building was across from there.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I don't even know what it's like over there.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I've worked there with the kids. I also worked where that Grayson lady worked. I don't know if she still works there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was it Job Corps?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Was it Job Corps? Job Corps. OK, OK.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: For a little while, it opened up the Child Welfare.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, Child Welfare. Yeah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: It opened.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You started there?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I worked there for 15 or 17 years. Then I realized I was getting old. When you worked there you didn't know what time you would be leaving, when they called you in. I worked there for a long time, and I knew I was getting old. I was starting to feel sad a little when I would take the kids somewhere. I was always worrying about the kids. After 16 years doing that, it was really hard to let those kids go. And it was hard to go get them. Then I started thinking about it a little to quit and retire.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you go get them from the parents sometimes?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Sometimes the kids would be doing good, and we had to take them back. It was the same thing, and I realized that it was getting hard for me, my heart.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess sometimes the kids would be crying when you would pick them up. No matter how bad they were treated, they still loved their parents.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: They did everything to them that they could. These days and a long time ago they did the same thing. There were things I saw that I've never seen before. But some of them were doing good, and really trying. Most of them weren't. I took out a lot of them that were bad off. I didn't want to take them back. But I had to try to take them back so they could get better. I believe the parents should raise them, but if they can't, then no.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many kids do you have?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Two, and I also have two grandkids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, did you raise boys?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: No, both of them were girls that I had. Both of my grandkids are girls, too. The oldest one passed away in nineteen fourteen from cancer. She graduated in May to be a nursing instructor. She was already an RN. I also had a strong belief in going to school. She was the oldest and graduated to be a nursing instructor. In January of nineteen fourteen she passed away, that one, but she graduated. She worked at Wilma P, she was an RN.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: RN, man. What about your parents? What were their names?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Nell and Waleli.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was your mother’s name?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Nell.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nell. What was your dad’s name in English?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Charlie.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Charlie?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: The one that works, Charlie Shell, is my brother.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, is that so, OK. Alright. The preacher, oh OK.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: There's another one living, it's been about two years, Freeman his name is. Ulewhedi was his name. He had diabetes and lost his leg. All of us kids have diabetes. They say it's hereditary, but I don't know how to say it in Cherokee: hereditary. We all have it. Our grandkids have already started that. I have one grandchild that already has diabetes. The mother also had diabetes, too. The oldest that passed away didn't have diabetes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your parents, where did they grow up? Your parents.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: My dad, just there in Stilwell. He grew up around there. My mom, probably Marble.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Marble City?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Towards Marble City, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess your dad was born around pretty close, yeah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Yeah, he was a deacon.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, what clan are you?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Wolf.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wolf, OK, Wolf. Tell me what that is? Wolf.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Wolves.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wolves, wolves, yeah. What were your parents’ parents’ names? What were their names?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Mom’s mother’s name was...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Mary.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Her name was Mary Watie.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Mary Watie was her name.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I didn't know her Cherokee name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your dad’s side?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Anawegi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Her name was Anawegi. OK.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Lucy Shell.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Lucy Shell.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Was the mother.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK Lucy Shell. I guess they were all raised up around there, close with all of you growing up.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Jack Shell was my grandpa’s name. He was a policeman.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A policeman?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Sallisaw. I mean Stilwell, a policeman.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Stilwell?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: There was a policeman in Sallisaw named Huckleberry Shell.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Huckleberry Shell was his name. Kawiya.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: And then there was...Luke Shell was another one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You all had to be good, there were police.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: That's why I grew up being nice.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did your late parents meet or find each other?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I don't know about that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They never talked about it?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They kept it a secret where they found each other.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I guess, I didn't know. I never did hear Dad talking about it. Both of them didn't talk about where they found each other.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I wonder why they kept it a secret. My parents did the same thing.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: That's it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That last name, Shell, where did that start from? Did they ever tell you? Where that started from?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I don't remember. Their dad’s name was Sam.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: His name was Sam Shell.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Sam Shell was his name, and his mother’s name was Lucy. And my mom’s dad’s name was Joe Chewey Seabolt.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Seabolt, oh, OK. Were you related to the late Sam Seabolt? He could really sing. Boy, you could hear him singing from a way. He was really loud. Yeah, I guess he's no longer with us?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was your husband’s name? You were married a long time ago.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I knew it, the Smiths. Rufus Smith, Jasper Smith and all of them. He was Rufus Smith’s son, was my husband, but I forget his Cherokee name. In English, it was Dewayne Smith.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: His name was Dewayne Smith.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh yeah, that was it. I knew him for a long time.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: That was my husband a long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you know his Cherokee name?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I knew it but I forgot.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I really forgot. When I leave here, I will remember it after a while.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That one brother coon, his name was Ahnigisdi, and Ben was Gwen and then Sam. I don't know his Cherokee name. I don't know the women’s names in Cherokee. I have heard his Cherokee name.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I really forgot, I'll be thinking about it all day long.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You're going to think about it later.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I'll be somewhere and remember it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: For instance, did you have a nickname growing up?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was it?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Don't you laugh either. Everybody and the church called me Bibitsi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Bibitsi, what does that mean?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I don't know, my aunt told the story when I was little as a child. I was the smallest baby born. They began calling me BB.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: BB.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I guess they were saying baby. Ended up Bibitsi, and till this day they call me that. There are two deacons at Chuculate that were in the army, Jim Proctor and Soldier Bunch. No matter where we were singing, they would say, “Bibitsi come here.” Here I would come. A long time ago, all the people in church would get on to you. They would say, “You're not supposed to do that.” They didn't mind telling you the truth, there was two deacons. I was really mean.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were always getting on to you?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: They were always getting on to me or sending me to the house all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they carry a switch? That's what they used to do to us. They carried a stick around and told us to go in.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: With a switch? We had to get our own switch, I would go get a skinny one. Then I found out that it hurts more. My dad never whipped me. He thought he was whipping me. He would roll up paper and hit me with that. He didn't whop us, as for myself, I don't remember him whipping me. For my mom, that's all she knew, go get a switch, go get a switch.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did your dad sing?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your mom?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Her, too, you're talking about Sam. Mom was like that. She really liked tobacco. They used to call her Nellie Tobacco, anywhere you could hear her singing for two miles. All of us were singers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Charlie sings, too, and Soldier Aniyosgi.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Me and Joyce, her name is Ahgtiyi, she was singing a lot. We got old. We don't sing anymore.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you help Charlie Shell and Soldier when they were singing?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK, they were really good singers. I guess Charlie still sings as good as always?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: He does, he sings good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Soldier Aniyosgi is starting to get sick now.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: All of us, I had open heart surgery at that time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So that broke it up.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: My singing changed.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where I'm from, Soldier Aniyosgi and his wife live there.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Yeah, I visit him. He's starting to get really sick.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: His wife is the same, sick, too.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: The same.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, what about your parents? Did they have good stories about what happened years ago, or something interesting about what they went through long ago? Did they tell you anything, or were they told anything?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Really, the thing that I thought was interesting that I've seen, when someone would die, they would help each other, and they would go there to spend the night. So the oldest girl, her name was Tsinisi, she would babysit us sometimes while they were helping out, sometimes for two days. After they would bury them, they would still stay to help out and clean up. They taught us the same. I thought that was amazing, they taught us the same. We were doing the same thing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was really like that, for three days you're not supposed to go anywhere when you've been to a funeral.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: That's what I thought was interesting.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They used to get some kind of grass after the funeral. They would do like that [gesture] and put it on theirselves. Did you ever see that?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Also, when our mother passed away, somebody came. He was from Jay, Kingfisher I think. Eli Stick.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, Eli Stick. I know him.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: That was Eli Stick.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I know him.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: He doctored the whole house. My late dad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, that's what he did. Also, some people use cedar limbs, they would put them under the house and smoke the house. When someone would pass away, that’s how they cleaned it, by smoking it out with cedar back then.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: My little sister, we call her little Nell, she was going to Texas, but her husband is a Kiowa. That's what he does, that powwow.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, powwow, yeah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: We call him Chow. Warren Quitone, that's my nephew, he does that, too. She married his dad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, like you're saying, those people used to be around. I guess there are still some around?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Yeah, also stomp grounds, the late Dewayne my husband, he would do that, too. He was Mose Smith’s grandchild.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Mose Smith, yeah, this is asking. Did anybody talk about the Trail of Tears, like how they came through or heard about how they came through, all of the Cherokees?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: They heard about people talking about it, but they haven't seen it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What were they saying when they heard about it?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Amazing Grace.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Amazing Grace, yeah that's a pretty song. Yeah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I wonder about that, you have to think about them. They went through rough times. Because I feel like because of them is why I'm alive. I'm thankful.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, we have it good now.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: They came through rough times.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh man, some are still there.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Yeah, sometimes I think about it, what if I was still there, and grew up there. What would it have been like? I think they talk different.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, yeah, when they talk about things, instead of saying dowalili, they will say digtuleni.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Yes, also I worked at Immersion for six or seven years, helped teach there. I really liked it. But I felt like I was traveling too far. I'm getting old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, oh yeah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I really liked it, but now the new teachers are saying it different. I don't know, I have a hard time understanding everything they're saying. When I was teaching, whenever they would say it different than me, I would tell them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, yeah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: What about you? Do you understand what they're saying?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Some of them I don't understand. Then I ask them what they are saying.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time a woman my wife knew, my wife had on a new blouse. She asked her in Cherokee where she got her blouse. The lady said, “Your blouse.” My wife said, “What?” The lady said, “Your blouse” in Cherokee. My wife said, “What is that?” The lady said, “What you're wearing.” My wife said, “Oh.” I don't know where that started from tsatitlidi. We were thinking a long time ago, it’s what they called tsatlidi, your shirt tsanuwo.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Tsatildi.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I never heard that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really? Yeah. They were talking to her in Cherokee and that's what she said.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: The people from North Carolina sang with us one time. They sang and we sang. They were at a little church going toward Westville Road. We would meet there to sing, they were from North Carolina. I wasn't back then, something was bothering him. Then I was asked tlake tsuga yigi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: tlake tsuga yigi.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I didn't understand what that was. I asked him, “What is that?” He said, “You're not married.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He said tsuga yigi.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Tsuga yigi. Us Cherokee, if we hear somebody say something different, we think it's funny. That's what happened to us. I told him, “No I'm not married.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was talking about a wedding ring.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Yeah, he was talking about my ring. I didn't know what to say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were you wondering what he was saying?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I didn't know what to think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about growing up? What was it like? Was it all woods, with a lot of trees standing?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: We were always playing in the woods, we didn't hardly ever get in the house. When somebody showed up, they would tell us to go play. We would find things to do ourselves. We were playing, because there were a lot of us running around playing ball, just anything, and fighting with each other. They would spank us, too. I think about how good I grew up, it wasn't like it is now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you all play outside at night, too?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: Outside, they would let us build a fire. No telling how long we would play outside. We weren't even scared, and now...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It's not good these days if a child is outside by themselves.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I don't understand the way kids are nowadays. But I'm thankful how I was raised. I tried hard to raise my kids. The oldest one passed away. She didn't have kids, this little one has two of my grandkids. I raised her the same way, it seems like she does it. If she says something wrong, I correct her really quick. I tell her, “You're not supposed to say that.” Sometimes she gets mad at me. I tell her not to say that. She's just a child.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That's true. You follow how you were taught. For instance, if you have grandkids, we tell our grandkids that sometimes. These things aren't good.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I do that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Be careful, when they go somewhere, stay close to your mom. Don't be alone, for instance, when they go to the store, stay close to your mom is what we tell them.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: That's what I tell the girls, this month on the eighth, one of them will be 21. The younger one will be 15. How it was, my parents had a strong belief because they didn't get educated. I don't know, but they worked hard raising us. They believed if we went to school, we would have it easier is what they thought. They would say, “You have to go to school.” Soldier would say, “Tell Mom I'm not going,” that he was sick. He would start slumping around. Mom would say wait on him. He started looking for something. She would be waiting for him till he found his jacket, till he got in. They had a hard belief, I did the same thing, the oldest was an RN and a nursing director, the youngest one worked for 17 years at Stilwell hospital working lab. She went to school for lab. She was in the lab.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me too. Our grandkids, my wife teaches them like you do. I don't know if you know the singers Creekkillers was the name. Creekkillers is the name. They're from the North. That's their kids, two girls and a boy. The boy is 22. He plays music. The girls are learning. One of the girls is learning the piano and the other guitar. They go around and play music sometimes. If someone passes, they call them. We’re always teaching them to listen to what their parents are telling them to do. Don't be asking us, ask them. They're your parents. That's your parents, we tell them. We love them. We will do anything for you all if it's the right thing, we tell them.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: The oldest would say, “I don't know why, Mom, that you get so mad at me that you would kill me.” In a little bit, you would talk nice to me. Me loving you never ends. It's never-ending. I told that I brought her into this world.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As for me, if they want something, I ask their parents. This is what they want, what do you all think? Sometimes they say no, and sometimes they tell us to just give it to them. We make it so the parents have to approve it, whether they allow it or not.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: That's right, when I tell them something I want them to do it. But sometimes they would get mad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes they would get on to them. We would tell them, “They're just teaching you the right things.”

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I would tell them the way I was raised.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you were growing up, it's asking this question. What kind of food did they raise and cook? What did you like the best? That your parents were cooking?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: What they cooked? The neck bone. Mom would cook those with cornbread.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gali, that's it, yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: My mouth fills up when I hear that. These days, my youngest grandchild, but they don't talk Cherokee. If I would've raised them, it wouldn't be that way. Both parents are Cherokees. But their dad was not taught Cherokee, and me, I married a white man, that's what made it hard. But the oldest one could talk Cherokee. But the little second one, no. She asked me the other day if I thought her child could learn Cherokee if she put her in the school here. I told her if she stayed with me, she would learn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She would have to learn.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: If she was going to learn it, she would learn it from me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about a long time ago in Cherokee, they would say asigi. Did you ever hear anything like that?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: All the time, I say that myself. Till this day when someone says something I'll say sgigi or I will say dohiuka.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If you say something happened to somebody, they say, hadewv. You probably heard all of that, too.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: If it was like that when I was growing up. Wow!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes it seemed like some of them didn't believe you. They would just be looking at you saying, “Oh really?”

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: We had an uncle that we just got to know, we called him uncle. We grew up calling him uncle. We were talking about him the other day. His name was Ada Bunch and he was a medicine man. He was a half-brother and I didn't know it. I grew up calling him uncle. I have a lot of uncles that didn't seem like uncles. This man came and stayed with us. He stayed with us for a year. When we went to school and got on the bus, he would have a fire going close to the bus in the winter, that's why he was the only one we called uncle. We didn't know him when he came to us. He was a real uncle to us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He really treated you good, didn't he?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: He was good to us, he was our babysitter. Everything, when we would be playing. He would always be sitting right there. He was cripple.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: We loved him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When he had to leave, I bet you all missed him.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I lived by the highway, my grandpa lived up on the hill. We grew up there and my dad built a new house. He would come and take us to church. When we would come back we would watch him go up the hill. He was a funny old man.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about this? These people from North Carolina talk different and naming things. What do you think of this school? Do they ever talk to you? Do you understand what they're saying?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I really have to pay attention before I can understand what they're saying. But I can understand, but I really have to pay attention to what they're saying. I'll misunderstand.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about our Cherokee language? Say about within the next 20 years, will it continue to fade away or end? That’s what it's asking us here. What do you think?

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I think, I believe it's going to end is what I think. And then these that are learning are going to meet and talk and understand each other is what I think. But like we talk.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It's not going to be that way.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I don't believe it's going to be that way. The way that they are learning, I believe they're going to meet and get together.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: For instance us talking. They're going to listen to us talking, and they might learn something. It will be great if they learn something from listening. Myself, I'm thankful that the teachers are still trying to teach Cherokee. I feel thankful if it continues.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I don't believe that how we're talking now will never be that way again. It's going to end.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well I'm glad we got to talk.

segments.speaker: ruby-jackson
segments.translation: I'm glad, too. Mitch, I appreciate it.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh OK.
